newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat-Serb vote looks split in ex-rebel counties.
newsitem.headline: Croat-Serb vote looks split in ex-rebel counties.

text.p: Croatia's ruling nationalist party won elections in one of two counties in a former rebel enclave but deadlocked with a minority Serb party in the other, according to unofficial, incomplete returns released on Friday.

A formal joint announcement of results by Croatia's state electoral commission and the temporary U.N. administrators of the enclave, Eastern Slavonia, failed to materialise for the second straight day.

The April 13-14 elections were plagued by technical irregularities on the first day but ran more smoothly on the second. U.N. officials said the delay in reporting results was caused by a complex tabulation process.

State television said unofficial, preliminary returns for the Osijek-Baranja County assembly showed President Franjo Tudjman's HDZ party with 44.4 percent, the opposition Croatian Social Liberal Party 21.47 percent, the Serb SDSS bloc 12.76 percent and the Croatian Peasant Party (HSS) 6.23 percent.
Parties must get 5 percent to qualify for assembly seats.

In Vukovar-Srijem County, the vote appeared to have split between the HDZ and SDSS, with 43 percent each, while 12 percent went to an independent list led by a Croatian ultra-rightist who used to be in the HDZ, television said.

Incomplete returns for one of the enclave's main towns, Beli Manastir, put the SDSS at 57 percent and an unspecified "Croatian option" -- presumably all Croatian parties combined -- at 43 percent, it said.

Available returns indicated that Croatian parties won majorities in two of the three biggest towns and in 17 of 26 municipalities in the enclave, it added. SDSS leaders earlier said they had won 11 districts.
"These results are not final becuase they have yet to be confirmed by the national election commission," said Petar Kljajic, head of the electoral commission in Osijek-Baranja.

Eastern Slavonia, seized by Serbs in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia, will return to central Croatian authority later this year after a transitional period as a U.N. protectorate.
Local Serbs have been guaranteed minority rights and were expected to form majority governments in some municipalities.
But ethnic hostility lingering from the war remains intense and some of the 120,000-odd Serbs in the region are expected to flee to Serbia instead of submit to renewed Croatian rule.

Croatian parties, especially the HDZ, were backed by 58,000 Croat refugees who were driven out of the enclave in fighting six years ago but now want to reclaim their homes, many of them occupied by Serbs displaced by war.
The elections coincided with voting for municipal and county assemblies throughout the rest of Croatia.

Tudjman's party regained control of almost all 21 county assemblies and most town councils but lost to or deadlocked with opposition coalitions in the more liberal big cities, including the capital Zagreb.

International observers said the elections were administered efficiently overall but voting in Eastern Slavonia was riddled with technical irregularities and opposition parties lacked proper access to the main state-run media.

Technical problems in Eastern Slavonia included last-minute changes of election regulations, inaccuracies in voter lists, late delivery and absence of materials including ballots and ballot boxes and late opening of polling stations.
